L568@P15: user-friendly technique into play as a potential case detection tool.
L569@P15: A recent Cochrane review has assessed the non-contact methods available to detect people at risk of
L570@P15: primary angle-closure glaucoma. Five non-invasive tests were studied. These comprised the oblique
L571@P15: flashlight test, LACD, AS-OCT, Scheimpflug photography and scanning peripheral anterior chamber
L572@P15: depth analyser (SPAC), all of which either measure or estimate the dimensions of the drainage angle.
L573@P15: The conclusion was that, although the quality of studies was sub-optimal, limbal anterior chamber
L574@P15: depth, a quick and simple test, has high sensitivity and specificity to diagnose angle-closure. The
L575@P15: authors did comment that the test could be useful for targeted screening in populations with a high
L576@P15: prevalence of the condition.
L577@P15: AS OCT, when available, is a very useful supplement. It creates a documentary record of the
L578@P15: examination finding which may be used in any subsequent triage or referral refinement.
L579@P15: In light of the evidence identifying a low risk of sight loss from glaucoma or pathology related to acute
L580@P15: angle-closure in people with occluded drainage angles, it is now advised that referrals be made in line
L581@P15: with NICE guidance (GC81) for raised IOP or glaucoma. Those with presumed occluded angles should only
L582@P15: be referred on the basis of elevated IOP, glaucoma, or the following risk factors constituting “PACS PLUS”.
L583@P15: “PACS PLUS”
L584@P15: Criteria for Referral of People with Suspected Occluded Angles to the Hospital Eye Service
L585@P15: Angle Criteria
L586@P15: Either – a limbal chamber depth grade < ¼ at the temporal limbus
L587@P15: Or – an anterior segment OCT showing irido-trabecular contact (ITC)
L588@P15: PLUS: one of the following criteria
L589@P15: • People with only one “good eye” in which deterioration of vision may threaten independent
L590@P15: living or livelihood
L591@P15: • Vulnerable adults who may not report ocular or vision symptoms
L592@P15: • Family history of significant angle closure disease
L593@P15: • High hypermetropia (> + 6.00 dioptres)
L594@P15: • Diabetes or another condition necessitating regular pupil dilation
L595@P15: • Those using antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action
L596@P15: • People either living in remote locations (such as foreign aid workers, armed forces stationed
L597@P15: overseas or oil rig workers etc.) where rapid access to emergency ophthalmic care is not possible
L598@P15: The finding of “PACS PLUS” should trigger referral to the Hospital Eye Service
L599@P15: “PACS MINUS”
L600@P15: If an individual has the angle-characteristics specified above but none of the “plus” criteria, and
L601@P15: does not meet NICE glaucoma referral guidelines, they should be advised to seek seek a regular
L602@P15: NHS sight test.
L603@P15-16: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 164.4 Management
L604@P16: v. What is the recommended management of primary angle-closure disease
L605@P16: The major advance in evidence informing the management of primary angle-closure disease comes
L606@P16: from the 2016 EAGLE randomised control trial (RCT) which enrolled patients with either primary angleclosure glaucoma (regardless of IOP) or primary angle-closure disease with a IOP >/= 30 mmHg and
L607@P16: randomised these participants to receive either clear lens phacoemulsification or laser iridotomy. This
L608@P16: trial showed that clear lens phacoemulsification was superior to laser iridotomy in terms of metrics of
L609@P16: disease control, the economic measures and patient reported outcomes. Clear lens phaco was resulted
L610@P16: in better IOP control to laser iridotomy. After 3 years, IOP was 1 mmHg lower in the phaco group but
L611@P16: with less medications (the rates of being off medication were 60% versus 20% in the two groups) and
L612@P16: less number of glaucoma surgeries (0.5% vs 11% in the phaco and laser PI group, respectively). Phaco
L613@P16: was cost-effective, showing cost savings in economic modelling. Quality of life remained stable in the
L614@P16: phaco group, but dropped in the LPI group.28 The question of whether goniosynechiolysis (GSL) provides
L615@P16: any supplementary benefit to phacoemulsification alone has been addressed in some RCTs which
L616@P16: showed no benefit to the additional use of the GSL.29,30
L617@P16: There is an evidence gap on the management of cases of angle-closure disease with IOP between
L618@P16: 21-29mmHg. In the absence of any specific evidence, standard care (laser iridotomy) should be offered,
L619@P16: with supplementary management judged on individual clinical need.
L620@P16: Effectiveness of LPI may decrease with greater severity of the disease. Studies showed that most
L621@P16: PACS eyes did not need any further intervention after LPI, while many PAC, PACG, and acute PAC eyes
L622@P16: required additional treatment to control IOP. The question of whether laser iridotomy location has any
L623@P16: bearing on the troubling side effect of dysphotopsia has been examined in three clinical trials which
L624@P16: showed opposing results. A small RCT carried out in Canada suggested that a temporal location of
L625@P16: iridotomy reduced rates of dysphotopsia symptoms31 while a larger study in India showed that no effect
L626@P16: of laser iridotomy site on the rate of dysphotopsia symptoms.32 There appears to be no difference in rate
L627@P16: of bleeding with discontinuation of anticoagulant treatment providing INR levels remain below 3.0.33
L628@P16: Laser peripheral iridoplasty has been proposed for eyes with remaining appositional angle closure after
L629@P16: LPI. Two RCT’s identified no benefit for IOP control for laser iridoplasty when used in addition to laser
L630@P16: iridotomy in PAC/PACG.34,35
L631@P16-17: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 17w. When to do a laser iridotomy in narrow angles/occludable angles/PACS
L632@P17: In a large RCT of screening for PACG carried out in Mongolia (N= 4,725), the population was enrolled
L633@P17: and underwent randomisation to either no intervention or to screening with measurement of central
L634@P17: anterior chamber depth. If screened participants met criteria for PACS, these people were offered laser
L635@P17: iridotomy. At the end of the study, incident glaucoma rates were compared between the intervention
L636@P17: (screened) and the untreated control group. This study showed that there was no difference in the
L637@P17: rate of new glaucoma between the control group and the screened group. In this context, the trial
L638@P17: concluded that there was no benefit for population-wide screening and prophylaxis for people at high
L639@P17: risk of PACG.36
L640@P17: The ZAP study, carried out in southern China, enrolled 11,991 people over the age of 50, and identified
L641@P17: 889 with PACS. These people were randomised to receive laser iridotomy in one eye and no treatment in
L642@P17: the other eye. Iridotomy halved the risk of new angle-closure disease (HR 0.53 over 6 years), i.e., raised
L643@P17: IOP and/or new PAS, but the rate of new disease in both treated and untreated eyes was very low (4.2
L644@P17: versus 8.0 cases of PACD per 1,000 eye years). Most cases were identified on the basis of new PAS, which
L645@P17: appeared to pose little immediate risk to loss of vision. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent
L646@P17: PAC (PAS, raised IOP, or very rare acute crises) was 44 over 6 years. There were no cases of incident
L647@P17: glaucoma identified in this trial in treated or untreated eyes, and no cases of severe visual impairment.
L648@P17: Using the best available data to extrapolate the NNT to prevent glaucoma, a projected figure of 126 to
L649@P17: prevent one case of glaucoma over 10 years. As the older Chinese population appears to be one of the
L650@P17: highest risk groups globally for PACG, it is reasonable to assume that the risk to the UK population (with
L651@P17: much lower prevalence and incidence of PACD) is no higher than that seen in ZAP. Whether the same
L652@P17: results are applicable to non-Chinese populations remains to be proven.
L653@P17: As preventive treatment was of minimal benefit numerically in the high-risk Chinese population, the
L654@P17: most logical conclusion here is that there is no benefit from large-scale prophylactic laser iridotomy
L655@P17: treatments in the UK. An economic analysis which attempts to extrapolate the ZAP data to the UK
L656@P17: NHS situation is underway, and will provide an additional perspective on the case for prophylaxis. A
L657@P17: sister study of ZAP, carried out in Singapore (ANALIS), has recently been completed. This study shows a
L658@P17: similar protective effect of laser iridotomy as ZAP (halving of risk), but that PACG, elevated IOP and AAC
L659@P17: Summary of evidence:
L660@P17: • Phacoemulsification lens extraction is preferred over laser PI for PAC disease with IOP >
L661@P17: 30mmHg (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong)
L662@P17: • Goniosynechialysis has been shown to have no benefit and therefore should not be carried
L663@P17: out (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L664@P17: • There is no need to stop anti-coagulants for PI when INR < 3
L665@P17: (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L666@P17: • Studies have shown no consistent evidence for PI location influencing dysphotopsia:
L667@P17: PI may be placed at either superior (12 o’clock) or temporal locations
L668@P17: (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L669@P17: • Residual ITC is common after PI (seen in 20-80% of cases). No evidence supports
L670@P17: further interventions for ITC alone. It may be used to risk-stratify follow-up after PI.
L671@P17: (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L672@P17: • Laser peripheral iridoplasty has been shown to have no IOP lowering benefit.
L673@P17: (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong)
L674@P17-18: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 18were uncommon in treated and untreated eyes over 5 years. The majority of disease endpoints were
L675@P18: PAS.37 On the basis of the medical data available currently, routinely offering prophylactic treatment to
L676@P18: all people classed as PACS is not currently advised. Laser PI may be advisable for people with high-risk
L677@P18: PACs (see below)
L678@P18: Heritability studies and molecular genetic studies outlined above suggest that PACD will cluster in
L679@P18: families. A natural assumption is that family members of those with PACD or PACG are at inherently
L680@P18: higher risk than other members of the population. However, this specific question has never been
L681@P18: addressed. People who require regular pharmacological dilation of the pupils for monitoring of retinal
L682@P18: disease are at increased risk of acute angle-closure crises.
L683@P18: Research need
L684@P18: • It is currently unclear if the finding of PAS indicates a significant risk of sight loss. An
L685@P18: observational study of the natural history of eyes with PAS is needed to determine if these people
L686@P18: should be monitored, or even identified.
L687@P18: • It is unknown if people who have a family history of PACD or who harbour a known genetic risk
L688@P18: variant are at higher risk of developing glaucoma (i.e. loss of vision) than the general population.
L689@P18: With the increasing availability of genetic testing, and the rise of “precision medicine”,
L690@P18: understanding the implications of heritable risk will be increasingly important.
L691@P18: Summary of evidence:
L692@P18: • There is no benefit in screening for (i.e. in attempting to detect precursors of, and
L693@P18: prevention of,) PACG in a high risk Asian populations.
L694@P18: (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong)
L695@P18: • Although a high-quality trial has shown laser PI reduces (halves) the risk of incident
L696@P18: PAC disease in high risk population (Chinese over the age of 50 years with PACS), the
L697@P18: risk of incident disease is small. Thus, most people are likely to receive little benefit from
L698@P18: prophylactic PI.
L699@P18: (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong)
L700@P18: • Until further evidence is forthcoming, laser PI IS advised for people with PACS PLUS
L701@P18: additional risk factor(s) such as an “only eye”, a family history of significant angle closure
L702@P18: disease, high hypermetropia, diabetes or another condition necessitating regular pupil
L703@P18: dilation, use of antidepressants or medication with an anticholinergic action, and those
L704@P18: people either living or working in remote locations (such as foreign aid workers, armed
L705@P18: forces stationed overseas or oil rig workers) where accessing emergency ophthalmic care is
L706@P18: not possible.
L707@P18: (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong)
L708@P18: • Laser PI IS NOT advised for most people with PACS with no additional risk factors.
L709@P18: (Evidence/recommendation: High; Strong)
L710@P18-19: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 19x. Laser iridotomy in the fellow eye of people suffering acute angle-closure
L711@P19: Contralateral fellow eyes of those which have suffered an acute attack are at high risk of suffering a
L712@P19: similar fate.38,39 Laser iridotomy appears effective in preventing long term IOP rises in around 90% of
L713@P19: these eyes.40 Although never subjected to an RCT, laser iridotomy is viewed as mandatory in the fellow
L714@P19: eye of those who have suffered and acute angle-closure crisis.41
L715@P19: Practice point
L716@P19: Anecdotally, ophthalmologists have encountered patients who have re-presented within days with
L717@P19: acute crises in their fellow eye when discharged without undergoing a laser iridotomy. It is therefore
L718@P19: strongly advised that laser iridotomy be attempted in the fellow eye without delay, before the patient is
L719@P19: discharged, once their IOP is controlled.
L720@P19: y. What is the recommended management of an acute angle-closure crisis
L721@P19: The acute management of an angle-closure crisis has been the subject of remarkably few randomised
L722@P19: controlled trials and therefore robust data on management is relatively sparse. However, the principles
L723@P19: for managing this relatively common ophthalmic emergency are not controversial.
L724@P19: Most patients will be in moderate to severe pain with acutely reduced vision. Nausea and vomiting
L725@P19: are relatively common. Therefore, the immediate priorities are analgesia, antiemesis and rapid
L726@P19: confirmation
L727@P19: of diagnosis, with subsequent topical and systemic medication to reduce the intraocular pressure.
L728@P19: The most important management decision must be confirming that angle-closure is present, and that
L729@P19: intraocular pressure is elevated. Once this has been established, it is crucial to exclude secondary
L730@P19: causes of angle-closure. If lens-induced or retro-lenticular mechanisms of angle-closure are not
L731@P19: recognised and treated appropriately with cycloplegia (i.e. atropine or cyclopentolate), the use of
L732@P19: topical pilocarpine will aggravate the condition and result in prolonged pain and a delay in controlling
L733@P19: intraocular pressure.
L734@P19: The key physical sign that will help to quickly identify a lenticular or retrolenticular secondary
L735@P19: mechanism is a marked asymmetry of the central anterior chamber depth. The only regularly-reported
L736@P19: scenario in which a bilateral presentation of angle-closure attributable to posteriorly segment
L737@P19: mechanisms is that associated with the use of topiramate causing supraciliary effusions and anterior
L738@P19: rotation of the ciliary body.42 Therefore, use of topiramate should be routinely sought on direct
L739@P19: questioning in suspected cases
L740@P19: of atypical angle-closure.
L741@P19: In acute angle-closure, regardless of whether this is thought to be pupillary block or non-pupil-block
L742@P19: plateau iris, the cardinal intervention is laser peripheral iridotomy, which should be done as quickly as
L743@P19: practically possible. Initial treatment with medication may be necessary for pain control, initial pressure
L744@P19: control, and to help achieve corneal clarity. The use of intensive pilocarpine drops is not advised. After
L745@P19: an initial instillation of pilocarpine, an appropriate dosage frequency would be every six hours. Other
L746@P19: topical glaucoma medication should be used as clinically indicated. Topical steroids should also be
L747@P19: Summary of evidence:
L748@P19: • Laser iridotomy IS recommended for all contralateral eyes when acute (symptomatic)
L749@P19: angle-closure has occurred in the fellow eye. This should be done at the time when the
L750@P19: acute angle-closure is treated. (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong)
L751@P19-20: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 20used to control inflammation. Probably the single most useful medical agent that should be employed
L752@P20: in the initial stages of pressure control is systemic acetazolamide. Before prescribing any medication, a
L753@P20: medical and allergy history should be taken. Allergies to sulphonamide medications such trimethoprim,
L754@P20: or severe nephropathy, would contra-indicate use of acetazolamide. Systemic acetazolamide is widely
L755@P20: used in the control of acutely elevated intraocular pressure; It is highly effective, and generally well
L756@P20: tolerated, although paraesthesia, polyuria and fatigue are common side effects. Severe side effects
L757@P20: from use of systemic acetazolamide are rare and largely confined to subgroups of patients.43 Particular
L758@P20: caution is advised relating to:
L759@P20: 1. Hypokalaemia in patients on thiazide diuretics or angiotensin-receptor blockers
L760@P20: 2. Metabolic acidosis in ‘sicker’ hospitalised patients
L761@P20: 3. Dyspnoea in patients that have already an increased work of breathing due to their underlying
L762@P20: condition
L763@P20: 4. Underlying HIV/cryptococcal meningitis – Two deaths in critically ill patients receiving
L764@P20: acetazolamide occurred in this setting
L765@P20: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) is a rare but severe and sometimes
L766@P20: fatal condition associated with exposure to medications, and has been reported in association with
L767@P20: acetazolamide treatment. However, acetazolamide appears well tolerated, even among patients
L768@P20: predisposed to SJS/TEN.44
L769@P20: Mannitol is used by some ophthalmologists to control intra-ocular pressure in a variety of clinical
L770@P20: scenarios, including in “acute” symptomatic cases of angle-closure, and in perioperative management
L771@P20: of eye with, or at risk of, glaucoma. However, a report to NHS Improvement (10.08.2017) found that
L772@P20: of 872 cases where mannitol had been used, serious adverse effects occurred at the following rates:
L773@P20: death 0.8% (N=7), death or severe harm 2.2% (N= 7+12), death or severe or moderate harm: 6.2% (N=
L774@P20: 7+12+35). Risks include dehydration, fluid overload and acute kidney injury. A subsequent poll of 5
L775@P20: Medication Safety Officers raised concerns about lack of guidance and lack of familiarity with risks of
L776@P20: this agent. If mannitol is used
L777@P20: for management of elevated intraocular pressure, the following procedures are advised:
L778@P20: 1. Fluid balance should be carefully recorded
L779@P20: 2. Renal function should be assessed prior to treatment, and monitored as clinically appropriate
L780@P20: 3. Only a single dose should be prescribed. A repeat dose should only be considered after
L781@P20: consultant review
L782@P20: 4. Dosing should be determined on the basis of weight and urinary output. Clinicians not familiar
L783@P20: with intravenous fluid management and assessment of renal function should take advice from
L784@P20: physicians
L785@P20-21: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 21Acute Angle Closure Care Pathway (pupillary block or plateau iris
L786@P21: mechanism)
L787@P21: If no/insufficient response by 2 hours, or technically not possible to do (cornea
L788@P21: oedematous) consider laser peripheral iridoplasty or diode laser cycloablation
L789@P21: (recommend all NHS Eye Depts with urgent care service have diode)
L790@P21: When PI complete, commence G. Dexamethasone 0.1% or G. Prednisolone 1%
L791@P21: at minimum of hourly while awake for 24 hours then 4 x day for one week
L792@P21: If laser iridotomy technically feasible (cornea clear, patient comfortable),
L793@P21: proceed to laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes
L794@P21: Examination to exclude to confirm elevated pressure from angle-closure, and
L795@P21: to identify/exclude secondary causes, lenticular and retro-lenticular causes
L796@P21: Review after 30-60 minutes
L797@P21: Identify any prior allergies/contraindications
L798@P21: Analgesia and anti-emesis if required
L799@P21: Stat medication
L800@P21: G. Dorzolamide 2%/G. Timolol 0.5% combination
L801@P21: G. Apraclonidine 0.5%
L802@P21: G. Pilocarpine 2%* (defer if IOP> 40 mmHg)
L803@P21: IV Acetazolamide 250mg (if IOP> 40mmHg)
L804@P21: Secondary cases should receive care directed at primary pathology
L805@P21: (e.g. drug-induced uveal effusions such as topiramate, neovascular and uveitic)
L806@P21: * Atropine 1% is substituted for pilocarpine if lenticular/retro-lenticular causes
L807@P21-22: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 22Practice point
L808@P22: An important safety point when deciding on treatment regimen would be to enquire about the presence
L809@P22: of coronary artery disease causing angina, prior myocardial infarction or a past history of coronary
L810@P22: artery stenting. All of these should be regarded as contraindications to the use of apraclonidine or
L811@P22: brimonidine.
L812@P22: The use of “argon”/green laser iridoplasty in early management of raised IOP for patients presenting
L813@P22: with acute angle-closure crises was studied in an RCT which randomised patients to receive either laser
L814@P22: iridoplasty or topical pilocarpine and timolol after all patients had received systemic acetazolamide.
L815@P22: The trial found that the intraocular pressure fell more quickly in the group that underwent laser
L816@P22: iridoplasty, but there was no difference between the two groups by two hours.45 The interpretation
L817@P22: of this trial differs around the world. There is no clear consensus that laser iridoplasty should be
L818@P22: deployed as an immediate management in acute angle closure. However, it could be used as a second
L819@P22: line treatment if the patient is unresponsive to topical medication and systemic acetazolamide after
L820@P22: two hours, and possibly for patients with hazy corneas (e.g., due to oedema) making laser iridotomy
L821@P22: technically not possible to conduct.
L822@P22: If a patient remains unresponsive to medication and laser iridoplasty, then diode laser cycloablation
L823@P22: treatment is frequently very effective in controlling intraocular pressure. Emergency trabeculectomy
L824@P22: is not advised. Limbal paracentesis has been reported as a management option which can rapidly
L825@P22: achieve intraocular pressure lowering. However, anecdotally, this technique can lead to severe
L826@P22: complications.
L827@P22: A randomized, controlled trial compared the efficacy of phacoemulsification and intraocular lens
L828@P22: implant (phaco/IOL) with laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) performed on people suffering AAC within 1
L829@P22: week of presentation. People who had responded to medical treatment such that intraocular pressure
L830@P22: (IOP) was ≤30 mmHg within 24 hours, and had cataract with visual acuity of ≤6/15 were enrolled. The
L831@P22: 2-year cumulative survival was 61% and 89% for the LPI and phaco/IOL groups, respectively (P = 0.034),
L832@P22: indicating that phaco/IOL may be superior to LPI in stabilizing IOP.46
L833@P22: Practice point
L834@P22: Consider the possibility of secondary (lenticular or retrolenticular) mechanisms of angle-closure. These
L835@P22: cases typically present with asymmetrical central anterior chamber depth. These cases should be
L836@P22: treated with mydriasis and not pilocarpine.
L837@P22-23: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 23In patients with co-existing cataract and angle-closure disease, lens extraction is the initial
L838@P23: treatment option for the management of early to moderate PACG.47, 48
L839@P23: Two small RCTs have compared phacoemulsification alone versus phacotrabeculectomy with
L840@P23: mitomycin-C for patients with PACG and cataract. A randomised controlled study on medically
L841@P23: controlled PACG with coexisting cataract, found that phacoemulsification alone was effective in
L842@P23: terms of decreasing IOP and reducing the requirements of postoperative glaucoma medications at
L843@P23: 2 years. There were no significant differences in terms of IOP, visual acuity and progression of visual
L844@P23: field between the two treatment groups. The phaco-trabeculectomy group required less topical
L845@P23: medications in the 2-year period compared to the phacoemulsification alone group but experienced
L846@P23: more complications.49
L847@P23: 4.5 Surgery
L848@P23: Summary of evidence:
L849@P23: • 1st Line: Medical treatment with systemic acetazolamide, topical pilocarpine and other
L850@P23: ocular hypotensive medication together should be given immediately in cases of acute
L851@P23: primary angle closure. Topical steroids, oral analgesia and antiemetics (as required) should
L852@P23: also be given.
L853@P23: • 2nd Line: Argon/green laser iridoplasty should be considered when medical treatment fails
L854@P23: to break the attack (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L855@P23: • Cyclodiode laser should be considered for cases refractory to both medical therapy and
L856@P23: ALPI. (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong)
L857@P23: • Laser iridotomy or surgical iridectomy should be attempted in both eyes following
L858@P23: resolution of the initial attack of acute angle closure (Evidence/recommendation: Low;
L859@P23: Strong)
L860@P23: • Paracentesis has no proven role in the management of acute angle closure and may cause
L861@P23: harm. (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong)
L862@P23: • In patients with cataract who experience acute angle closure, early phacoemulsification
L863@P23: should be offered once intraocular pressure is controlled and the cornea is clear,
L864@P23: approximately 1 to 4 weeks after presentation. (Evidence/recommendation: Low; Strong)
L865@P23: Summary of evidence:
L866@P23: • Clear lens phaco is superior to PI and is advised as primary intervention in PACG.
L867@P23: (Evidence/recommendation: High: Strong)
L868@P23: • Phacoemulsification and goniosynechialysis (GSL) surgery does not reduce need for antiglaucoma eyedrops versus phaco alone (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L869@P23: • Phacoemulsification clear lens extraction/cataract surgery is preferred to
L870@P23: trabeculectomy and phaco-trab in PACG on the basis of safety, but trabeculectomy or
L871@P23: phacotrabeculectomy may be considered for severe disease (Evidence/recommendation:
L872@P23: Moderate; Weak)
L873@P23: • Early phaco may be of more benefit than PI in patients with AAC and PACG with cataract
L874@P23: (Evidence/recommendation: Moderate; Weak)
L875@P23-24: The Management Of Angle-Closure Glaucoma 24For medically uncontrolled PACG with coexisting cataract, phaco-trabeculectomy gave lower
L876@P24: postoperative IOP and lower glaucoma medication usage than phacoemulsification alone in the 2-year
L877@P24: follow-up period. However, phaco-trabeculectomy was again associated with more complications
L878@P24: compared to phacoemulsification alone.50
L879@P24: Clear lens extraction (CLE) can be considered for the initial management of mild to moderate PACG,
L880@P24: as well as PAC with IOP > 30 mmHg, for patients over 50 years of age. In the EAGLE trial, CLE resulted
L881@P24: in slightly better IOP lowering, reduced medication use and subsequent glaucoma surgery, improved
L882@P24: quality of life, and cost effectiveness compared to LPI. As the study was carried out in the UK and East
L883@P24: Asia, the implications for non-Chinese/non-European populations are uncertain. Additionally, it should
L884@P24: be noted that lens extraction can be more complicated intraoperatively and postoperatively than for
L885@P24: routine eyes.
L886@P24: In medically uncontrolled PACG eyes without cataract, trabeculectomy with mitomycin C may be
L887@P24: indicated, particularly in younger patients with accommodative ability. In a small RCT comparing
L888@P24: the efficacy of phacoemulsification versus trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C in medically
L889@P24: uncontrolled PACG eyes with clear lens, trabeculectomy group was found to be more effective than
L890@P24: phacoemulsification, requiring on average 1.1 fewer drugs after surgery. Surgical complications were
L891@P24: substantially higher in the trabeculectomy group than among those undergoing phacoemulsification
L892@P24: (44% vs. 4% respectively). There were no differences between the two treatment groups in number of
L893@P24: additional surgical interventions at 2 years, although one third of patients undergoing trabeculectomy
L894@P24: developed significant cataract within this timeframe.51
L895@P24: However, in cases of advanced PACG, uncontrolled IOP and concurrent cataract, primary
L896@P24: trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C may be a viable option. The sequence of cataract and glaucoma
L897@P24: surgery need to be considered carefully. The benefits of sequential surgery versus combined phacotrabeculectomy in more severe or advanced disease remain unclear.
